content: Influenza epidemics predominantly occur during the winter months and are responsible for an average of approximately 20,000 deaths annually in the United States. Influenza viruses can also cause pandemics, during which the rates of illness and mortality from influenza-related complications can rise dramatically on a global scale. These viruses affect individuals across all age groups, with the highest infection rates observed among children. However, the most severe illnesses and deaths occur among individuals aged over 65 years and those of any age with underlying medical conditions that increase their risk of complications from influenza. Vaccination against influenza is the primary method for preventing the disease and its severe complications. It is particularly recommended for individuals aged over 65 years, healthcare workers, and household members who frequently interact with high-risk individuals, as they can transmit the virus to those at greater risk. Vaccination has been shown to reduce influenza-related respiratory illnesses, physician visits, hospitalizations, and deaths among high-risk populations. It also decreases otitis media in children and reduces work absenteeism in adults. Despite significant increases in influenza vaccination rates during the 1990s, further improvements are needed, especially among high-risk individuals under 65 years of age. Strategies to enhance vaccination coverage include implementing reminder/recall systems and standing orders programs. While vaccination remains the cornerstone of influenza prevention and control, antiviral medications are also recommended as an adjunct to vaccination, particularly for chemoprophylaxis and treatment. Influenza A and B viruses are the primary types responsible for human epidemics. Influenza A viruses are further categorized into subtypes based on two surface antigens: hemagglutinin (H) and neuraminidase (N). Influenza B viruses are not divided into subtypes. Since 1977, influenza A (H1N1), A (H3N2), and influenza B viruses have been in global circulation. Recently, influenza A (H1N2) viruses, likely resulting from genetic reassortment between human A (H3N2) and A (H1N1) viruses, have been detected in multiple countries. Both influenza A and B viruses undergo antigenic drift, which involves point mutations during viral replication, leading to the emergence of new antigenic variants. This antigenic drift is the virologic basis for seasonal epidemics and necessitates the inclusion of new strains in the annual influenza vaccine. Influenza viruses are primarily transmitted from person to person through respiratory droplets produced by coughing and sneezing. The incubation period is typically 1–4 days, with an average of 2 days. Adults and children are infectious from the day before symptom onset until approximately 5 days after illness onset, although children and immunocompromised individuals may shed the virus for longer periods. Common symptoms include fever, myalgia, headache, severe malaise, nonproductive cough, sore throat, and rhinitis. Influenza-related respiratory illness can be challenging to distinguish from other respiratory pathogens based on symptoms alone. Clinical definitions for influenza-like illness, which include fever and cough, have reported sensitivities ranging from 63% to 78% and specificities from 55% to 71% compared to viral culture. Influenza illness typically resolves within a few days for most individuals, although cough and malaise may persist for over two weeks. However, complications such as secondary bacterial pneumonia, primary influenza viral pneumonia, or co-infections with other pathogens can occur, particularly in individuals with underlying pulmonary or cardiac disease. Influenza infection has also been associated with encephalopathy, transverse myelitis, Reye syndrome, myositis, myocarditis, and pericarditis. The risk of complications, hospitalizations, and deaths from influenza is highest among individuals aged over 65 years, very young children, and those with underlying health conditions. Hospitalization rates vary by age group and epidemic severity, with the highest rates observed among children aged 0–4 years and individuals over 65 years. During influenza epidemics from 1969–1970 through 1994–1995, the estimated number of influenza-associated hospitalizations in the United States ranged from approximately 16,000 to 220,000 per epidemic. On average, 114,000 influenza-related excess hospitalizations occurred annually, with 57% of these hospitalizations involving individuals under 65 years of age. Influenza-related deaths can result from pneumonia or exacerbations of cardiopulmonary conditions and other chronic diseases. Older adults account for over 90% of deaths attributed to pneumonia and influenza. During 19 of 23 influenza epidemics, estimated rates of influenza-associated deaths ranged from approximately 30 to over 150 deaths per 100,000 persons aged over 65 years. The increasing number of older individuals in the population may contribute to a rise in pneumonia and influenza deaths in the United States. Vaccination of high-risk individuals before the seasonal increase in influenza virus circulation is the most effective means of reducing the impact of influenza. Vaccination coverage can be increased by administering vaccines during hospitalizations or routine healthcare visits before the influenza season, thereby eliminating the need for special visits to physicians' offices or clinics. Vaccination in institutional settings, such as nursing homes, can reduce the risk of outbreaks by inducing herd immunity. Vaccination of healthcare workers and close contacts of high-risk individuals can also reduce influenza transmission and subsequent complications. The effectiveness of the influenza vaccine depends on the recipient's age, immune status, and the antigenic similarity between vaccine strains and circulating viruses. Most vaccinated children and young adults develop high post-vaccination antibody titers, which are protective against illness caused by similar strains. When vaccine and circulating viruses are antigenically similar, the vaccine prevents influenza illness in approximately 70%–90% of healthy adults under 65 years of age. Vaccination also reduces work absenteeism and healthcare resource use, including antibiotic prescriptions, when vaccine strains match circulating viruses. Children as young as six months can develop protective antibody levels after vaccination, although responses may be lower among high-risk children. Studies have demonstrated vaccine efficacy rates ranging from 56% to 91% against influenza respiratory illness in children, depending on age and health status. Among elderly individuals, vaccine efficacy in preventing hospitalization for pneumonia and influenza ranges from 30% to 70%, with higher effectiveness in preventing severe illness and death among nursing home residents. Influenza vaccination is cost-effective, reducing healthcare costs and productivity losses associated with influenza illness. Economic studies have reported societal cost savings and substantial reductions in hospitalizations and deaths among vaccinated individuals aged over 65 years. Further studies are needed to evaluate the long-term costs and benefits of annual vaccination among children and adults under 65 years of age. Vaccination coverage among individuals aged over 65 years increased significantly during the 1990s, surpassing the Healthy People 2000 goal of 60%. However, coverage rates among racial and ethnic minorities remain lower than those among non-Hispanic whites. Strategies to achieve the Healthy People 2010 goal of 90% vaccination coverage for individuals aged over 65 years and to reduce disparities in vaccine coverage are needed. Increasing vaccination rates among high-risk individuals under 65 years of age, including children, is a priority for expanding influenza vaccine use. Annual vaccination is also recommended for healthcare workers to reduce absenteeism and protect high-risk patients. In summary, influenza vaccination is strongly recommended for individuals aged over six months who are at increased risk for complications from influenza. Healthcare workers and close contacts of high-risk individuals should also be vaccinated to reduce transmission. Vaccination can be administered to any individual aged over six months to reduce the likelihood of influenza infection.
